nodes.name: Poset of degree sequences via nonzero homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\rho_d$ and $\rho_{d'}$ be extremal rays of the cone of Betti diagrams for $S$ corresponding to Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively. Then $\rho_d \preceq \rho_{d'}$ if and only if there exist Cohen--Macaulay modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_S(M',M)_{\leq 0}\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $\rho_d\preceq\rho_{d'}$ holds exactly when some Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions of types $d,d'$ admit a nonzero degree-$\le 0$ homomorphism $M'\to M$.
assumptions: Let $\rho_d$ and $\rho_{d'}$ be extremal rays of the cone of Betti diagrams for $S$ corresponding to Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively.
conclusions: $\rho_d \preceq \rho_{d'}$ if and only if there exist Cohen--Macaulay modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_S(M',M)_{\leq 0}\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Poset of root sequences via nonzero homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\rho_f$ and $\rho_{f'}$ be extremal rays of the cone of cohomology tables for $\PP^{n-1}$ corresponding to supernatural sheaves of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively. Then $\rho_f\preceq \rho_{f'}$ if and only if there exist supernatural sheaves $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\PP^{n-1}}(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $\rho_f\preceq\rho_{f'}$ holds exactly when some supernatural sheaves of types $f,f'$ admit a nonzero homomorphism $\EE'\to\EE$.
assumptions: Let $\rho_f$ and $\rho_{f'}$ be extremal rays of the cone of cohomology tables for $\PP^{n-1}$ corresponding to supernatural sheaves of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively.
conclusions: $\rho_f\preceq \rho_{f'}$ if and only if there exist supernatural sheaves $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\PP^{n-1}}(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Equivariant poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional $\Bbbk$-vector space with $\ch(\Bbbk)=0$, and let $\rho_d$ and $\rho_{d'}$ be the extremal rays of the cone of Betti diagrams for $S=\Sym(V)$ corresponding to finite length modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$. Then $\rho_d\preceq \rho_{d'}$ if and only if there exist finite length $\GL(V)$-equivariant modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(M',M)_{\le 0}\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic-zero equivariant analogue: $\rho_d\preceq\rho_{d'}$ iff some finite length $\GL(V)$-equivariant modules with pure resolutions admit a nonzero equivariant homomorphism.
assumptions: let $\rho_d$ and $\rho_{d'}$ be the extremal rays of the cone of Betti diagrams for $S=\Sym(V)$ corresponding to finite length modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$.
conclusions: $\rho_d\preceq \rho_{d'}$ if and only if there exist finite length $\GL(V)$-equivariant modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(M',M)_{\le 0}\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Equivariant poset of root sequences
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional $\Bbbk$-vector space with $\ch(\Bbbk)=0$, and let $\rho_f$ and $\rho_{f'}$ be the extremal rays of the cone of cohomology tables for $\PP^{n-1} = \PP(V)$ corresponding to supernatural vector bundles of types $f$ and $f'$. Then $\rho_f\preceq \rho_{f'}$ if and only if there exist $\GL(V)$-equivariant supernatural vector bundles $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic-zero equivariant analogue for supernatural vector bundles: $\rho_f\preceq\rho_{f'}$ iff a nonzero $\GL(V)$-equivariant homomorphism exists.
assumptions: let $\rho_f$ and $\rho_{f'}$ be the extremal rays of the cone of cohomology tables for $\PP^{n-1} = \PP(V)$ corresponding to supernatural vector bundles of types $f$ and $f'$.
conclusions: $\rho_f\preceq \rho_{f'}$ if and only if there exist $\GL(V)$-equivariant supernatural vector bundles $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Relative subtlety of the two main theorems
nodes.statement: Though the statements of these two theorems are quite parallel, Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main} is far more subtle than Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:root:main}. Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:root:main} follows nearly directly from the Eisenbud--Schreyer pushforward construction of supernatural sheaves, but without modification, it is not clear how to compare the modules constructed in~\cite[\S5]{EiScConjOfBS07}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The degree-sequence theorem is much harder than the root-sequence theorem, whose proof follows from the Eisenbud--Schreyer pushforward construction.

nodes.name: Modules of types $d=(0,2,3,5)$ and $d'=(0,3,9,10)$ over $\PP^2$
nodes.statement: We illustrate this via an example. Let $n=3$, $d=(0,2,3,5)$, $d'=(0,3,9,10)$, and $M$ and $M'$ be finite length modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, as constructed in~\cite[\S5]{EiScConjOfBS07}. We know of no method to produce a nonzero element of $\Hom(M,M')_{\leq 0}$, even in this specific case. The difficulty here stems from differences in the constructions of $M$ and $M'$: the module $M$ is constructed by pushing forward a complex of projective dimension $5$ along $\PP^2\times (\PP^1)^2\to \PP^2$, whereas $M'$ is constructed by pushing forward a complex of projective dimension $10$ along $\PP^2\times \PP^2\times \PP^5\to\PP^2$. Thus, the construction of~\cite[\S5]{EiScConjOfBS07} does not even suggest that Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main} ought to be true.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Two Eisenbud--Schreyer modules of types $(0,2,3,5)$ and $(0,3,9,10)$ built from different projections, for which no nonzero homomorphism is apparent.

nodes.name: Key ideas behind the proof of the degree-sequence theorem
nodes.statement: Our motivation for conjecturing the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main} -- and the first key idea behind its proof -- is based on a flexible version of the Eisenbud--Schreyer construction of pure resolutions. This is Construction~\ref{modif:es} below, and we show that the basic results of~\cite[\S5]{EiScConjOfBS07} can be adapted to this construction. This extension enables us to use a single projection map to simultaneously produce modules $N$ and $N'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$. In the case under consideration, we construct both $N$ and $N'$ by pushing forward complexes of projective dimension $10$ along the projection map $\PP^2\times (\PP^1)^7\to \PP^2$.\footnote{We note that $M\ne N$ and $M'\ne N'$ in this example.} We may then produce elements of $\Hom(N,N')_{\leq 0}$ by working with the complexes on the source $\PP^2\times (\PP^1)^7$ of the projection map. However, finding such a nonzero element poses a second technical challenge in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main}. This requires an explicit and somewhat delicate computation involving the pushforward of a morphism of complexes along the projection $\PP^2\times (\PP^1)^7\to \PP^2$. This computation is carried out in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:deg:after:reduction}, thus providing a new understanding of how certain modules with pure resolutions are related.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A single projection from a product of $\PP^1$'s produces both modules simultaneously; a delicate pushforward computation then produces the nonzero map.

nodes.name: Finite length as the equivariant analogue of Cohen--Macaulay
nodes.statement: The action of $\GL(V)$ has two orbits on the maximal ideals of $S$: one consisting of the maximal ideal $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and the other consisting of its complement. An equivariant Cohen--Macaulay module therefore has only two options for its support, and hence either has finite length or must be a free module. Thus the finite length hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:equivariant:deg} is the natural equivariant analogue of the Cohen--Macaulay hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Since $\GL(V)$ has two orbits on maximal ideals, an equivariant Cohen--Macaulay module is finite length or free, so finite length is the right equivariant hypothesis.

nodes.name: Difficulty of the equivariant degree-sequence statement
nodes.statement: As above, the statement for pure resolutions is more subtle than the corresponding statement for supernatural vector bundles. The modules constructed in \cite[\S 3]{efw} do not have nonzero equivariant homomorphisms between them, but the explicit combinatorics of the representation theory involved suggests a minor modification which does work. This also suggests how the maps should be defined in terms of the explicit presentation of the modules; the remaining nontrivial step is to show that these maps are in fact well-defined. The main obstacle is that such maps must be compatible with the actions of both the general linear group and the symmetric algebra, and the interplay between the two is delicate. This key issue in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:equivariant:deg} is accomplished through a careful computation involving Pieri maps (combined with results from~\cite{sam}).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The EFW modules admit no nonzero equivariant maps, but a combinatorial modification does; well-definedness is settled via Pieri maps.

nodes.name: Graded Betti number
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a finitely generated graded $S$-module. The \defi{$(i,j)$th graded Betti number} of $M$, denoted $\beta_{i,j}(M)$, is $\dim_\Bbbk \mathrm{Tor}_i^S(\Bbbk, M)_j$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences

nodes.name: Betti diagram
nodes.statement: The \defi{Betti diagram} of $M$ is a table, with rows indexed by $\ZZ$ and columns by $0, \dots, n$, such that the entry in column $i$ and row $j$ is $\beta_{i,i+j}(M)$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
differentia: with rows indexed by $\ZZ$ and columns by $0, \dots, n$
the entry in column $i$ and row $j$ is $\beta_{i,i+j}(M)$

nodes.name: Degree sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence $d=(d_0, \dots, d_n)\in \left( \ZZ\cup \{\infty\} \right)^{n+1}$ is called a \defi{degree sequence} for $S$ if $d_i>d_{i-1}$ for all $i$ (with the convention that $\infty>\infty$).
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences

nodes.name: Length of a degree sequence
nodes.statement: The \defi{length} of $d$, denoted $\ell(d)$, is the largest integer $t$ such that $d_t$ is finite.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences

nodes.name: Pure resolution of type $d$
nodes.statement: A graded $S$-module $M$ is said to have a \defi{pure resolution of type $d$} if a minimal free resolution of $M$ has the form \[ 0\leftarrow M \leftarrow S(-d_0)^{\beta_{0,d_0}} \leftarrow S(-d_1)^{\beta_{1,d_1}} \leftarrow \dots \leftarrow S(-d_{\ell(d)})^{\beta_{\ell(d),d_{\ell(d)}}} \leftarrow 0. \qedhere \]
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: $M$ has a pure resolution of type $d$ when its minimal free resolution has exactly one twist $S(-d_i)$ in each homological degree $i$.
differentia: has the form $0\leftarrow M \leftarrow S(-d_0)^{\beta_{0,d_0}} \leftarrow S(-d_1)^{\beta_{1,d_1}} \leftarrow \dots \leftarrow S(-d_{\ell(d)})^{\beta_{\ell(d),d_{\ell(d)}}} \leftarrow 0$

nodes.name: Existence of Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement: For every degree sequence $d$, there exists a Cohen--Macaulay module with a pure resolution of type $d$~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~0.1} (see also~\cite{boij-sod1}*{Conjecture~2.4}, \cite{efw}*{Theorem~0.1}).
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.origin_citation: Eisenbud & Schreyer 2009, Thm. 0.1; Boij--Söderberg, Conj. 2.4; Eisenbud--Fløystad--Weyman, Thm. 0.1
conclusions: there exists a Cohen--Macaulay module with a pure resolution of type $d$

nodes.name: Positive decomposition of Betti diagrams into pure diagrams
nodes.statement: The Betti diagram of any finitely generated $S$-module can be written as a positive rational combination of the Betti diagrams of Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions (see ~\cite {EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~0.2} and~\cite{BoijSoderbergNonCM08}*{Theorem~2}).
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.origin_citation: Eisenbud & Schreyer 2009, Thm. 0.2; Boij & Söderberg 2008 (non-CM case), Thm. 2
conclusions: The Betti diagram ... can be written as a positive rational combination of the Betti diagrams of Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions

nodes.name: Cone of Betti diagrams
nodes.statement: The \defi{cone of Betti diagrams} for $S$ is the convex cone inside $\bigoplus_{j \in \ZZ}\QQ^{n+1}$ generated by the Betti diagrams of all finitely generated $S$-modules. Each degree sequence $d$ corresponds to a unique extremal ray of this cone, which we denote by $\rho_d$, and every extremal ray is of the form $\rho_d$ for some degree sequence $d$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
differentia: generated by the Betti diagrams of all finitely generated $S$-modules

nodes.name: Partial order on degree sequences
nodes.statement: For two degree sequences $d$ and $d'$, we say that $d\preceq d'$ and that $\rho_d\preceq \rho_{d'}$ if $d_i\leq d_i'$ for all $i$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences

nodes.name: Simplicial fan structure induced by the partial order on degree sequences
nodes.statement: This partial order induces a simplicial fan structure on the cone of Betti diagrams, where simplices correspond to chains of degree sequences under the partial order $\preceq$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences

nodes.name: Nonzero homomorphism implies comparability of degree sequences
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $M'$ be graded Cohen--Macaulay $S$-modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively. If $\Hom(M',M)_{\leq 0}\ne 0$, then $d\preceq d'$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero degree-$\le 0$ map $M'\to M$ between Cohen--Macaulay modules with pure resolutions forces $d\preceq d'$.
assumptions: Let $M$ and $M'$ be graded Cohen--Macaulay $S$-modules with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively.

nodes.name: Proof of the reverse implication for degree sequences
nodes.statement: Write $\ell' = \ell(d')$ and $\ell = \ell(d)$. If $\ell' > \ell$, then $\codim M' > \codim M$, and, by~\cite{BrHe:CM}*{Propositions~1.2.3 and~1.2.1}, $\Hom(M', M) = 0$. Therefore we may assume that $\ell' \leq \ell$. By hypothesis, we may fix a nonzero homomorphism $\phi \in \Hom(M',M)_t$ for some $t\leq 0$. Let $F_\bullet$ and $F'_\bullet$ be minimal graded free resolutions of $M$ and $M'$, respectively, and let $\left\{ \phi_i\colon F'_i \to F_i \right\}_{i \geq 0}$ be the comparison maps in a lifting of $\phi$. Suppose by way of contradiction that there is a $j$ such that $d'_j < d_j$. Since $d'_j < d_j$, we see that $\phi_j = 0$. Hence, each $\phi_i$ such that $j \leq i \leq \ell'$ can be made zero by some homotopy equivalence. Write $(-)^\vee = \Hom_S(-, S(-n))$. Since $M$ and $M'$ are Cohen--Macaulay, we note that $(F_\bullet)^\vee$ and $(F'_\bullet)^\vee$ are minimal graded free resolutions of $\Ext^\ell_S(M,S(-n))$ and $\Ext^{\ell'}_S(M', S(-n))$. Further, the maps $\{\phi_i^\vee\}_{i \geq 0}$ define an element of $\Ext^{\ell-\ell'}_S\left(\Ext_S^\ell(M, S(-n)), \Ext_S^{\ell'}(M', S(-n))\right)$. In fact, if we write $N = \coker \left((F_{\ell'-1})^\vee \longrightarrow (F_{\ell'})^\vee\right)$, then $(\phi_{\ell'})^\vee \colon N \longrightarrow \Ext_S^{\ell'}(M', S(-n)))$ is the zero homomorphism. Hence $\phi_i^\vee = 0$ for all $0 \leq i \leq \ell'$, and therefore $\phi = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: if $d'_j<d_j$ the lifted comparison map vanishes in degree $j$, and dualizing with $\Hom_S(-,S(-n))$ forces $\phi=0$.

nodes.name: Codimension case $\ell'>\ell$
nodes.statement: Write $\ell' = \ell(d')$ and $\ell = \ell(d)$. If $\ell' > \ell$, then $\codim M' > \codim M$, and, by~\cite{BrHe:CM}*{Propositions~1.2.3 and~1.2.1}, $\Hom(M', M) = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of the case $\ell'>\ell$, where $\Hom(M',M)=0$ by a codimension comparison.

nodes.name: Lift the homomorphism to the resolutions
nodes.statement: Therefore we may assume that $\ell' \leq \ell$. By hypothesis, we may fix a nonzero homomorphism $\phi \in \Hom(M',M)_t$ for some $t\leq 0$. Let $F_\bullet$ and $F'_\bullet$ be minimal graded free resolutions of $M$ and $M'$, respectively, and let $\left\{ \phi_i\colon F'_i \to F_i \right\}_{i \geq 0}$ be the comparison maps in a lifting of $\phi$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Fix a nonzero $\phi$ of degree $t\le 0$ and lift it to comparison maps $\phi_i\colon F'_i\to F_i$.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis kills $\phi_j$
nodes.statement: Suppose by way of contradiction that there is a $j$ such that $d'_j < d_j$. Since $d'_j < d_j$, we see that $\phi_j = 0$. Hence, each $\phi_i$ such that $j \leq i \leq \ell'$ can be made zero by some homotopy equivalence.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Assume $d'_j<d_j$ for some $j$; then $\phi_j=0$ and all later $\phi_i$ can be homotoped to zero.

nodes.name: Dualize the resolutions
nodes.statement: Write $(-)^\vee = \Hom_S(-, S(-n))$. Since $M$ and $M'$ are Cohen--Macaulay, we note that $(F_\bullet)^\vee$ and $(F'_\bullet)^\vee$ are minimal graded free resolutions of $\Ext^\ell_S(M,S(-n))$ and $\Ext^{\ell'}_S(M', S(-n))$. Further, the maps $\{\phi_i^\vee\}_{i \geq 0}$ define an element of $\Ext^{\ell-\ell'}_S\left(\Ext_S^\ell(M, S(-n)), \Ext_S^{\ell'}(M', S(-n))\right)$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Apply the duality $(-)^\vee=\Hom_S(-,S(-n))$, using Cohen--Macaulayness to keep the dual complexes resolutions.

nodes.name: Conclude that $\phi=0$
nodes.statement: In fact, if we write $N = \coker \left((F_{\ell'-1})^\vee \longrightarrow (F_{\ell'})^\vee\right)$, then $(\phi_{\ell'})^\vee \colon N \longrightarrow \Ext_S^{\ell'}(M', S(-n)))$ is the zero homomorphism. Hence $\phi_i^\vee = 0$ for all $0 \leq i \leq \ell'$, and therefore $\phi = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: The dual map vanishes on the cokernel, so every $\phi_i^\vee=0$ and hence $\phi=0$, the desired contradiction.

nodes.name: Necessity of the Cohen--Macaulay hypothesis
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:half:poset:deg} is untrue if we do not assume that $M'$ is Cohen--Macaulay. For example, consider $S = \Bbbk[x,y]$, $M = S/\langle x^2\rangle $, and $M' = S \oplus \Bbbk$. We used the hypothesis that $M'$ is Cohen--Macaulay to have that $\codim M' = \ell(d')$ and that $\Hom_S(F'_\bullet, S(-n))$ is a resolution.
nodes.section: 2 The poset of degree sequences
nodes.statement_short: Without Cohen--Macaulayness of $M'$ the proposition fails, e.g. $M=S/\langle x^2\rangle$, $M'=S\oplus\Bbbk$ over $\Bbbk[x,y]$.

nodes.name: Necessity of considering $\Hom(M',M)_{\leq 0}$ for $n=2$
nodes.statement: For instance, if $n=2, d=(0,1,2)$, and $d'=(1,2,3)$, then any $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$ will be isomorphic to $\Bbbk^m$ and $\Bbbk(-1)^{m'}$, respectively, for some integers $m,m'$. In this case, $\Hom(M',M)_0=0$, whereas $\Hom(M',M)_{-1}\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: For $d=(0,1,2)\preceq d'=(1,2,3)$ the degree-$0$ Hom vanishes while the degree-$(-1)$ Hom does not.

nodes.name: Reduction to degree-zero homomorphisms by shifting $d'$
nodes.statement: However, it is possible to reduce to the consideration of $\Hom(M',M)_0$. To do this, let $t := \min \{d'_i - d_i \mid d'_i\neq \infty \}$. By replacing $d'$ by $d' - (t,\dots,t)$, the forward direction of Theorem~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main} is an immediate corollary of the following result.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Shifting $d'$ by $t=\min\{d'_i-d_i\}$ reduces the forward direction of the main theorem to the degree-$0$ statement.

nodes.name: Existence of a degree-zero nonzero homomorphism after reduction
nodes.statement: Let $d \preceq d'$ be degree sequences for $S$ with $d_j = d'_j$ for some $0 \leq j \leq \ell(d')$. Then there exist finitely generated graded Cohen--Macaulay modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom(M',M)_0\ne 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: If $d\preceq d'$ agree in one position, some Cohen--Macaulay modules of those pure types admit a nonzero degree-$0$ map $M'\to M$.
assumptions: Let $d \preceq d'$ be degree sequences for $S$ with $d_j = d'_j$ for some $0 \leq j \leq \ell(d')$.
conclusions: there exist finitely generated graded Cohen--Macaulay modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom(M',M)_0\ne 0$.

nodes.name: The homomorphism group is nonzero only for special choices of modules
nodes.statement: The homomorphism group in Theorems~\ref{thm:poset:deg:main} and~\ref{thm:deg:after:reduction} is nonzero only for specific choices of the modules $M$ and $M'$. For two degree sequences $d \preceq d'$, there exist many pairs of modules $M$, $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, such that $\Hom(M',M)_{\leq 0}=0$. For example, take $d=d'=(0,2,4)$, $M = S/\< x^2,y^2 \>$, and $M' = S/\< l_1^2,l_2^2 \>$ for general linear forms $l_1$ and $l_2$. As another example, consider $d = (0,3,6) \prec d'= (0,4,8)$. When $M = S/\< x^3,y^3 \>$ and $M' = S/\< f,g \>$ for general quartic forms $f$ and $g$, we again have $\Hom(M',M)_{\leq 0}=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Many pairs of modules with pure resolutions of comparable types still have $\Hom(M',M)_{\leq 0}=0$; the theorem only asserts existence.

nodes.name: Two-step outline of the proof
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:deg:after:reduction} is given at the end of this section and involves two main steps. \begin{enumerate} \item Construct twisted Koszul complexes $\KK_\bullet$ and $\KK_{\bullet}'$ on a product $\PP$ of projective spaces (including a copy of $\PP^{n-1}$) and push them forward along the projection $\pi\colon \PP\to \PP^{n-1}$. This yields pure resolutions $F_\bullet$ and $F_\bullet'$ of types $d$ and $d'$ that respectively resolve modules $M$ and $M'$. \item Show that there exists a morphism $h_\bullet\colon \KK'_\bullet \to \KK_\bullet$ such that the induced map $\nu_\bullet \colon F_\bullet' \to F_\bullet$ is not null-homotopic. This yields a nonzero element $\psi\in \Hom_S(M', M)_0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Step 1: push forward twisted Koszul complexes to get pure resolutions; Step 2: produce a morphism whose pushforward is not null-homotopic.

nodes.name: How the construction is obtained from Eisenbud--Schreyer
nodes.statement: We achieve \eqref{eq:deg:step:1} by modifying the construction of pure resolutions by Eisenbud and Schreyer \cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{\S5}. We replace their use of $\prod_i \PP^{d_i - d_{i-1}}$ with a product of copies of $\PP^1$. This enables us to simultaneously construct pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$ and a nonzero map between the modules they resolve. The details of \eqref{eq:deg:step:1} are contained in Construction~\ref{modif:es}. For \eqref{eq:deg:step:2}, we apply Construction~\ref{modif:es} so as to produce the morphism $h_\bullet$. Checking that the induced map $\nu_\bullet$ is not null-homotopic uses, in an essential way, the hypothesis that $d_j = d'_j$ for some $0 \leq j \leq \ell(d')$. Example~\ref{ex:degseqs} demonstrates these arguments. Write $\PP^{1 \times r}$ for the $r$-fold product of $\PP^1$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: The Eisenbud--Schreyer factors $\prod_i\PP^{d_i-d_{i-1}}$ are replaced by copies of $\PP^1$, allowing both resolutions to be built at once.

nodes.name: Choice of the number $r$ of $\PP^1$ factors
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: $r$ is the maximum of $d_{\ell(d)}-d_0-\ell(d)$ and $d'_{\ell(d')}-d_0-\ell(d')$.

nodes.name: Modification of the Eisenbud--Schreyer construction of pure resolutions
nodes.statement: The objects involved in this construction of a pure resolution $F_\bullet$ of type $d$ will be denoted by $\Kos^d_\bullet$, $\KK_\bullet$, and $\cL$. The corresponding objects for the pure resolution $F'_\bullet$ of type $d'$ are $\Kos^{d'}_\bullet$, $\KK'_\bullet$, and $\cL'$. Let \begin{equation} r :=\max\{d_{\ell(d)}-d_0-\ell(d), d'_{\ell(d')}-d_0-\ell(d')\} \end{equation} and $\PP := \PP^{n-1}\times \PP^{1\times r}$. On $\PP$, fix the coordinates \[ \left([x_1:x_2:\dots:x_n], [y^{(1)}_0:y^{(1)}_1], \ldots, [y^{(r)}_0:y^{(r)}_1]\right) \] and consider the multilinear forms \[ f_p := \sum_{i_0 + \cdots + i_r = p} \left( x_{i_0}\cdot \prod_{j=1}^r y_{i_j}^{(j)} \right) \qquad \text{for } p = 1,2,\dots,n+r. \] (Note that $i_0 \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ and $i_j \in \{0,1\}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq r$.) We now define \begin{align*} D & := \{d_0, d_0+1, \dots, d_0+\ell(d)+r\}, & D' & := \{d_0, d_0+1, \dots, d_0+\ell(d')+r\}, \\ \delta & := (\delta_1< \dots< \delta_r) = D \minus d, & \delta' & := (\delta'_1< \dots< \delta'_r) = D' \minus d', \\ a & := \delta - (d_0+1, \ldots, d_0+1), & a' & := \delta' - (d_0+1, \ldots, d_0+1),& \\ \cL & := \cO_\PP(-d_0,a), \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{and} & \cL' & := \cO_\PP(-d_0,a'). \end{align*} (We view $\delta$ and $\delta'$ as ordered sequences.) Let $\Kos^{d}_\bullet$ be the Koszul complex on $f_1, \dots, f_{\ell(d)+r}$, which is an acyclic complex of sheaves on $\PP$ of length $\ell(d)+r$ (see \cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Proposition~5.2}). Let $\KK_\bullet := \Kos^d_\bullet \otimes \cL$. Let $\pi\colon\PP \rightarrow \PP^{n-1}$ denote the projection onto the first factor. By repeated application of~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Proposition~5.3}, $\pi_*\KK_\bullet$ is an acyclic complex of sheaves on $\PP^{n-1}$ of length $\ell(d)$ such that each term is a direct sum of line bundles. Taking global sections of this complex in all twists yields the pure resolution $F_\bullet$ of a graded $S$-module (that is finitely generated and Cohen--Macaulay). We can write the free module $F_i$ explicitly as follows. If $s=\max\{i \mid a_i-d_j+d_0 \leq -2\}$, then we have \[ F_j = S(-d_j)^{\binom{\ell(d)+r}{d_j-d_0}}\otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=1}^s \Hs^1(\PP^1, \cO(a_i-d_j+d_0)) \right) \otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=s+1}^r \Hs^0(\PP^1, \cO(a_i-d_j+d_0)) \right) . \] Let $\Kos^{d'}_\bullet$ be the Koszul complex on $f_1, \dots, f_{\ell(d')+r}$ and $\KK_\bullet' := \Kos^{d'}_\bullet \otimes \cL'$, and define $F'_\bullet$ in a similar manner.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the choices of $r$, $a$ and $a'$
nodes.statement: The value of $r$ in \eqref{equation:rForKos} is the least integer such that we are able to fit both the twists $-d_0$ and $\min\{-d_{\ell(d)}, -d'_{\ell(d')}\}$ in the $\PP^{n-1}$ coordinate of the bundles of the complexes $\KK_\bullet$ and $\KK'_\bullet$. The choices of $a$ and $a'$, which ensure that $F_\bullet$ and $F'_\bullet$ are pure of types $d$ and $d'$, are dictated by the homological degrees in $\KK_\bullet$ and $\KK_\bullet'$ that need to be eliminated in each projection away from a $\PP^1$ component of $\PP$. We then have \begin{align*} F_j & = S(-d_j)^{\binom{\ell(d)+r}{d_j-d_0}}\otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=1}^s \Hs^1(\PP^1, \cO(a_i-d_j+d_0)) \right) \otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=s+1}^r \Hs^0(\PP^1, \cO(a_i-d_j+d_0)) \right) \; \text{and} \\ F'_j & = S(-d_j)^{\binom{\ell(d')+r}{d_j-d_0}}\otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=1}^{s} \Hs^1(\PP^1, \cO(a'_i-d_j+d_0)) \right) \otimes \left( \bigotimes_{i=s+1}^{r} \Hs^0(\PP^1, \cO(a'_i-d_j+d_0)) \right), \end{align*} where both $F_j$ and $F'_j$ have the same number of factors involving $\Hs^0$ (and therefore also the same number involving $\Hs^1$). Hence we can repeatedly apply~\cite{explicit}*{Lemma 7.3} to conclude that $\nu_j$ is simply the map induced on cohomology by the map $h_{d_j-d_0}\colon \mathcal K_{d_j-d_0}'\to \mathcal K_{d_j-d_0}$.

nodes.statement_short: Since $s=s'$, the tensor factors of $F_j$ and $F'_j$ match, so Lemma 7.3 identifies $\nu_j$ with the cohomology map induced by $h$.

nodes.name: Choose the explicit monomial $h$
nodes.statement: We now fix a specific value of $h$ and show that $\nu_{j}\ne 0$. Let $c:=a-a'\in \mathbb N^r$ and write $c=(c_1, \dots, c_r)$. Let \[ h:=\left(y_0^{(1)} \right)^{c_1} \cdot \left(y_0^{(2)} \right)^{c_2} \cdots \left(y_0^{(r)} \right)^{c_r} =\mathbf{y}^{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c_1& \dots& c_r\\ 0&\dots &0\end{smallmatrix}\right)}, \] so that $h$ is the unique monomial of multidegree $(0,c)$ that involves only the $y_0^{(i)}$-variables.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Specialize $h$ to the unique monomial of multidegree $(0,c)$ in the $y_0^{(i)}$ variables.

For $I=\{i_1<\dots <i_{d_j-d_0}\}$ a subset of either $\{1, \dots, \ell(d)+r\}$ or $\{1, \dots, \ell(d')+r\}$, we use the notation $\epsilon_I:=\epsilon_{i_1}\wedge \dots \wedge \epsilon_{d_j-d_0}$ to write $S$-bases for $S(-d_j)^{ inom{\ell(d)+r}{d_j-d_0}}$ and for $S(-d_j)^{ inom{\ell(d')+r}{d_j-d_0}}$. nodes.name: Standing hypotheses for the equivariant module construction
nodes.statement: Throughout this section, we assume that $\Bbbk$ is a field of characteristic 0 and that all degree sequences have length $n$. Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional $\Bbbk$-vector space, and let $S = \Sym(V)$. We use $\Sc_\lambda$ to denote a Schur functor, as in Section~\ref{sec:equiv:root}.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic $0$, degree sequences of length $n$, $V$ of dimension $n$, and $S=\Sym(V)$.

nodes.name: Reduction of the equivariant theorem by a shift of $d'$
nodes.statement: As in Section~\ref{sec:construct deg}, a shift of $d'$ reduces the remaining direction of Theorem~\ref{thm:equivariant:deg} to the following result.

nodes.name: Equivariant modules with a nonzero degree-zero homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $d \preceq d'$ be two degree sequences such that $d_k = d'_k$ for some $k$. Then there exist finite length $\GL(V)$-equivariant $S$-modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(M',M)_0 \ne 0$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Equivariant analogue of the reduced theorem: comparable degree sequences agreeing in one spot admit equivariant modules with a nonzero degree-$0$ equivariant map.
assumptions: Let $d \preceq d'$ be two degree sequences such that $d_k = d'_k$ for some $k$.
conclusions: there exist finite length $\GL(V)$-equivariant $S$-modules $M$ and $M'$ with pure resolutions of types $d$ and $d'$, respectively, with $\Hom_{\GL(V)}(M',M)_0 \ne 0$.

nodes.name: Pieri's rule for tensoring a Schur functor with a symmetric power
nodes.statement: This proof will repeatedly appeal to Pieri's rule for decomposing the tensor product of a Schur functor by a symmetric power. We refer the reader to \cite[\S1.1 and Theorem 1.3]{sam} for a statement of this rule, as our main use of it will be through \cite[Lemma 1.6]{sam}.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Pieri's rule decomposes a Schur functor tensored with a symmetric power; used through Sam--Weyman Lemma 1.6.
nodes.origin_citation: Sam & Weyman, Pieri resolutions for classical groups, \S1.1, Thm. 1.3 and Lemma 1.6

nodes.name: The equivariant module $M(d)$ and its highest weights $\lambda(d)_j$
nodes.statement: Given a degree sequence $d$, let $M(d)$ be the $\GL(V)$-equivariant graded $S$-module constructed in~\cite{efw}*{\S3} (see also \cite{sam}*{\S2.1}), and let ${\bf F}(d)_\bullet$ be its $\GL(V)$-equivariant free resolution. By construction, the generators for each $S$-module ${\bf F}(d)_j$ form an irreducible $\GL(V)$-module whose highest weight we call $\lambda(d)_j$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: $M(d)$ denotes the EFW equivariant module of type $d$, with ${\bf F}(d)_j$ generated by the irreducible of highest weight $\lambda(d)_j$.

nodes.name: Nonzero equivariant morphism when $d'$ increases $d$ by one
nodes.statement: Let $d = (d_0, \dots, d_n) \in \ZZ^{n+1}$ be a degree sequence, and let $d'$ be the degree sequence obtained from $d$ by replacing $d_i$ by $d_i+1$ for some $i$. Then there exists an equivariant nonzero morphism $\phi \colon M(d')\otimes V\to M(d)$. Further, if $F_\bullet$ and $F_\bullet'$ are the minimal free resolutions of $M(d)$ and $M(d')\otimes V$ respectively, then we may choose $\phi$ so that the induced map $F_j'\to F_j$ is surjective for all $j\ne i$.

nodes.statement_short: Raising a single entry of $d$ by one produces a nonzero equivariant map $M(d')\otimes V\to M(d)$ that is surjective on $F_j$ for $j\ne i$.

let $d'$ be the degree sequence obtained from $d$ by replacing $d_i$ by $d_i+1$ for some $i$

nodes.name: Effect on the highest weights of raising one entry of $d$
nodes.statement: Let $d$ and $d'$ be degree sequences as in the statement of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules}. We observe that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $\lambda(d')_i = \lambda(d)_i$. \item If $j < i$, then $\lambda(d')_j$ is obtained from $\lambda(d)_j$ by removing a box from the $i$th part. \item If $j > i$, then $\lambda(d')_j$ is obtained from $\lambda(d)_j$ by removing a box from the $(i+1)$st part. \end{enumerate} For instance, if $d=(0,2,4)$ and $d'=(0,3,4)$, then we have \[ \lambda(d)_j=\begin{cases} (1,0) & \text{ if } j=0\\ (3,0) & \text{ if } j=1\\ (3,2) & \text{ if } j=2 \end{cases} \quad \text{ and } \quad \lambda(d')_j=\begin{cases} (0,0) & \text{ if } j=0\\ (3,0) & \text{ if } j=1\\ (3,1) & \text{ if } j=2. \end{cases} \qedhere \]
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Raising $d_i$ by one leaves $\lambda_i$ unchanged and removes one box from the $i$th (resp. $(i+1)$st) part for $j<i$ (resp. $j>i$).

nodes.name: Use of Sam--Weyman Lemma 1.6 for co-Pieri maps
nodes.statement: In the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules}, we repeatedly use~\cite{sam}*{Lemma 1.6}. The statement of the lemma is for factorizations of Pieri maps into simple Pieri maps $\Sc_\nu V \to \Sc_\eta V \otimes V$, but we need to factor into simple Pieri maps as well as simple co-Pieri maps $\Sc_\eta V \otimes V \to \Sc_\nu V$. No modification of the proof is needed: we simply use the fact that the composition of a co-Pieri map and a Pieri map of the same type is an isomorphism and that in each case that we apply~\cite{sam}*{Lemma 1.6}, the Pieri maps may be factored so that the simple Pieri maps and simple co-Pieri maps of the same type appear consecutively.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Sam--Weyman Lemma 1.6 extends to co-Pieri maps without modifying its proof.

nodes.statement:
Set $\lambda_\ell = \sum_{j=\ell}^{n-1} (d_{j+1} - d_j - 1)$ for $1 \le \ell \le n-1$, $\lambda_n = 0$, $\mu_1 = \lambda_1 + d_1 - d_0$, and $\mu_\ell = \lambda_\ell$ for $1 \le \ell \le n$. If $i = n$, we modify $\lambda$ and $\mu$ by adding 1 to all of its parts (so in particular, $\lambda_n = \mu_n = 1$). As in~\cite{efw}*{\S3}, define $M$ to be the cokernel of the Pieri map \[ \psi_{\mu / \lambda} \colon S(-d_1) \otimes \Sc_\mu V 	o S(-d_0) \otimes \Sc_\lambda V. \] We will choose partitions $\lambda'$ and $\mu'$ so that $M'$ is the cokernel of the Pieri map \[ \psi_{\mu' / \lambda'} \colon S(-d'_1) \otimes \Sc_{\mu'} V 	o S(-d'_0) \otimes \Sc_{\lambda'} V. \] To do this, we separately consider the three cases $i=0$, $i=1$, and $i \ge 2$. In each case, we specify $\lambda'$ and $\mu'$ (these descriptions are special cases of Remark~ef{remark:eqvtefw}) and construct a commutative diagram of equivariant degree 0 maps  egin{equation} \xymatrix{ S(-d_1) \otimes \Sc_\mu V \ar[rr]^-{\psi_{\mu/\lambda}} & & S(-d_0) \otimes \Sc_\lambda V \ S(-d'_1) \otimes \Sc_{\mu'} V \otimes V \ar[rr]^-{ \psi_{\mu' / \lambda'} \otimes 1_V} \ar[u]^-{\phi_\mu} & & S(-d'_0) \otimes \Sc_{\lambda'} V \otimes V \ar[u]^-{\phi_\lambda} } \end{equation} that induces an equivariant degree 0 map of the cokernels $\phi \colon M' 	o M$. Since the Pieri maps are only well-defined up to a choice of nonzero scalar, we only prove that the square commutes up to a choice of nonzero scalar. One may scale appropriately to obtain strict commutativity. Finally, after handling the three separate cases, we prove that the induced maps $F_j'	o F_j$ are surjective whenever $j
e i$. Since $F_ ullet'$ is a minimal free resolution, this implies that the map $F_ ullet'	o F_ ullet$ is not null-homotopic, and hence $\phi \colon M'	o M$ is nonzero. ~ 
oindent \emph{Case $i=1$.} Set $\lambda'_1 = \lambda_1 - 1$, $\lambda'_j = \lambda_j$ for $2 \le j \le n$, and $\mu' = \mu$. Also, let $d'_0 = d_0$ and $d'_1 = d_1 + 1$. Let $\phi_\lambda$ be the projection of $\Sc_{\lambda'} V \otimes V 	o \Sc_\lambda V$ tensored with the identity of $S(-d_0)$. From the degree $d_1 + 1$ part of \eqref{eqn:square}, we obtain \[ \xymatrix{ \Sym^1 V \otimes \Sc_\mu V \ar[r]^-\alpha & \Sym^{d_1 - d_0 + 1} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V \ \Sc_\mu V \otimes V \ar[r]^-\delta \ar[u]^- eta & \Sym^{d_1 - d_0 + 1} V \otimes \Sc_{\lambda'} V \otimes V \ar[u]^-\gamma. } \] Note that $\alpha$ is the linear part of ${ f F}_1 	o { f F}_0$ and is hence injective because $d_2 - d_1 > 1$. Since $ eta$ is an isomorphism, $\alpha  eta$ is injective. Also we have $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2$ because $d_2 - d_1 > 1$, so by Pieri's rule, every summand of $\Sc_\mu V \otimes V$ is also a summand of $\Sym^{d_1 - d_0 + 1} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V$. Using~\cite{sam}*{Lemma~1.6}, one can show that $\gamma \delta$ is also injective. Since the tensor product $\Sym^{d_1 - d_0 + 1} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V$ is multiplicity-free by the Pieri rule, this implies that these maps are equal after rescaling the image of each direct summand of $\Sc_\mu V \otimes V$ by some nonzero scalar. Hence this diagram is commutative, and the same is true for \eqref{eqn:square}. ~ 
oindent \emph{Case $i \ge 2$.} Set $\lambda'_i = \lambda_i - 1$ and $\lambda_j = \lambda_j$ for $j 
e i$. Similarly, set $\mu'_i = \mu_i - 1$ and $\mu'_j = \mu_j$ for $j 
e i$. Using the notation of \eqref{eqn:square}, let $\phi_\mu$ be a nonzero projection of $\Sc_{\mu'} V \otimes V$ onto $\Sc_\mu V$ tensored with the identity on $S(-d_1)$. Similar to the previous case, choose a nonzero projection $\Sc_{\lambda'} V \otimes V 	o \Sc_\lambda V$ and tensor it with the identity map on $S(-d_0)$ to get $\phi_\lambda$. From the degree $d_1$ part of \eqref{eqn:square}, we obtain \[ \xymatrix{ \Sc_\mu V \ar[r]^-\alpha & \Sym^{d_1 - d_0} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V \ \Sc_{\mu'} V \otimes V \ar[r]^-\delta \ar[u]^- eta & \Sym^{d_1 - d_0} V \otimes \Sc_{\lambda'} V \otimes V \ar[u]^-\gamma. } \] Let $\Sc_
u V$ be a direct summand of $\Sc_{\mu'} V \otimes V$. If $
u 
e \mu$, then $\Sc_
u V$ is not a summand of $\Sym^{d_1 - d_0} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V$, as otherwise we would have $
u_i = \lambda_i - 1$, and both of the compositions $\alpha  eta$ and $\gamma \delta$ would therefore be 0 on such a summand. If $

e i$, we now prove the surjectivity of the maps $F_j'	o F_j$, which implies that $\phi$ is a nonzero morphism, as observed above. nodes.statement: Set $\lambda_\ell = \sum_{j=\ell}^{n-1} (d_{j+1} - d_j - 1)$ for $1 \le \ell \le n-1$, $\lambda_n = 0$, $\mu_1 = \lambda_1 + d_1 - d_0$, and $\mu_\ell = \lambda_\ell$ for $1 \le \ell \le n$. nodes.name: Plan: commuting square in three cases, then surjectivity
nodes.statement: To do this, we separately consider the three cases $i=0$, $i=1$, and $i \ge 2$. Since $F_\bullet'$ is a minimal free resolution, this implies that the map $F_\bullet'\to F_\bullet$ is not null-homotopic, and hence $\phi \colon M'\to M$ is nonzero.

nodes.name: Case $i=1$
nodes.statement: \noindent \emph{Case $i=1$.} Set $\lambda'_1 = \lambda_1 - 1$, $\lambda'_j = \lambda_j$ for $2 \le j \le n$, and $\mu' = \mu$. Also, let $d'_0 = d_0$ and $d'_1 = d_1 + 1$. e \mu$, then $\Sc_
u V$ is not a summand of $\Sym^{d_1 - d_0} V \otimes \Sc_\lambda V$, as otherwise we would have $
u_i = \lambda_i - 1$, and both of the compositions $\alpha  eta$ and $\gamma \delta$ would therefore be 0 on such a summand. If $
u = \mu$, then the composition $\alpha  eta$ is nonzero, so it is enough to check that the same is true for $\gamma \delta$; this holds by~\cite{sam}*{Lemma~1.6}, and hence this diagram and \eqref{eqn:square} are commutative.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: For $i\ge 2$, summand-by-summand analysis of $\Sc_{\mu'}V\otimes V$ shows both compositions agree.

nodes.name: Case $i=0$ by duality
nodes.statement: \noindent \emph{Case $i=0$.} Set $d^\vee:= (-d_n, -d_{n-1}, \dots, -d_0)$ and $d'^{\vee}:=(-d'_n, -d'_{n-1}, \dots, -d'_0)$. Since $d_j=d_j'$ for all $j\ne i=0$, we see that $d^\vee$ and $d'^\vee$ only differ in position $n$. Hence, by the case $i\geq 2$ above (we assume that $n \ge 2$ since the $n=1$ case is easily done directly), we have finite length modules $M(d^\vee)$ and $M(d'^{\vee})$ with pure resolutions of types $d^\vee$ and $d'^\vee$, respectively, along with a nonzero morphism $\psi \colon M(d^\vee)\otimes V \to M(d'^\vee)$. If we define $N^\vee:= \Ext^n(N,S),$ then $M(d'^\vee)^\vee \cong M(d')$ and $(M(d^\vee)\otimes V)^\vee \cong M(d) \otimes V^*$ (both isomorphisms are up to some power of $\bigwedge^n V$ which we cancel off). In addition, since $\Ext^n(-,S)$ is a duality functor on the space of finite length $S$-modules, we obtain a nonzero map \[ \psi^\vee \colon M(d')\to M(d)\otimes V^*. \] By adjunction, we then obtain a nonzero map $M(d')\otimes V\to M(d)$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $i=0$ to the case $i\ge 2$ for the dual sequences, then dualize with $\Ext^n(-,S)$ and use adjunction.

nodes.name: Surjectivity of $F_j' \to F_j$ for $j \ne i$
nodes.statement: Fixing some $j\ne i$, we now prove the surjectivity of the maps $F_j'\to F_j$, which implies that $\phi$ is a nonzero morphism, as observed above. The key observation is that, in each of the above three cases, $F_j$ is an irreducible Schur module. Since $d_j=d_j'$, the map \[ F_j'=S(-d'_j)\otimes \Sc_{\lambda(d')_j}V\otimes V\to F_j=S(-d_j)\otimes \Sc_{\lambda(d)_j}V \] is induced by a nonzero equivariant map $\Sc_{\lambda(d')_j}V\otimes V\to \Sc_{\lambda(d)_j}V$. Since the target is an irreducible representation, this morphism, and hence the map $F_j'\to F_j$, is surjective. More specifically, the map $\Sc_{\lambda(d')_j}V\otimes V\to \Sc_{\lambda(d)_j}V$ is a projection onto one of the factors in the Pieri rule decomposition of $\Sc_{\lambda(d')_j}V\otimes V$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Irreducibility of the target makes $F_j'\to F_j$ a Pieri projection, hence surjective, so $\phi\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Equivariant resolutions for $d=(0,2,4)$ and $d'=(0,3,4)$
nodes.statement: This example illustrates the construction of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} when $d=(0,2,4)$ and $d'=(0,3,4)$. When writing the free resolutions, we simply write the Young diagram of $\lambda$ in place of the corresponding graded equivariant free module. Also, we follow the conventions in \cite{efw} and \cite{sam} and draw the Young diagram of $\lambda$ by placing $\lambda_i$ boxes in the $i$th {\it column}, rather than the usual convention of using rows. The morphism from Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} yields a map of complexes, which we write as \[ \begin{CD} @.M@<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|}} @<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|||}} @<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{,|,||}} @<<< 0 \\ @. _{\psi} @AAA@AAA @AAA @AAA \\ @. M'@<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|}}\otimes \varnothing @<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|}} \otimes {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|||}} @<<< {\tiny \tableau[scY]{|}} \otimes {\tiny \tableau[scY]{,|||}} @<<< 0.\\ \end{CD} \] Observe that $d_2=4=d_2'$ and that the vertical arrow in homological position $2$ is surjective, as it corresponds to a Pieri rule projection. A similar statement holds in position $0$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Young-diagram picture of the map of equivariant resolutions for $d=(0,2,4)\preceq d'=(0,3,4)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the equivariant module theorem
nodes.statement: Set $r:=\sum_{j=0}^n d_j'-d_j$. We may construct a sequence of degree sequences $d=:d^0<d^1<\dots <d^r:=d'$ such that $d^j$ and $d^{j+1}$ satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} for any $j$. Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} yields a nonzero morphism \[ \phi^{(j+1)} \colon M(d^{j+1})\otimes V\to M(d^j) \] for any $j=1, \dots, r$. If we set $M^{(j)}:=M(d^j)\otimes V^{\otimes j}$, and we set $\psi^{(j+1)}$ to be the natural map \[ \psi^{(j+1)} \colon M^{(j+1)}\to M^{(j)} \] given by $\phi^{(j)}\otimes \text{id}_V^{\otimes j}$, then we may compose the map $\psi^{(j+1)}$ with the map $\psi^{(j)}$. Let $M:=M^{(0)}=M(d),$ and let $M':=M^{(r)}=M(d')\otimes V^{\otimes r}$. We then have an equivariant map $\psi:=\psi^{(1)}\circ \dots \circ \psi^{(r)} \colon M'\to M$, and we must finally show that $\psi$ is nonzero. Let $F^{(j)}_\bullet$ be the minimal free resolution of $M^{(j)}$. Since $d_k=d_k'$, it follows that $d^{(j)}_k=d^{(j+1)}_k$ for all $j$. Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} then implies that we can choose each $\phi^{(j+1)}$ such that the map $\psi^{(j+1)}$ induces a surjection $F^{(j+1)}_k\to F^{(j)}_k$. Since the composition of surjective maps is surjective, it follows that the map $F^{(r)}_k\to F^{(0)}_k$ induced by $\psi$ is surjective. Since $F^{(0)}_\bullet$ is a minimal free resolution, we conclude that the map of complexes $F^{(r)}_\bullet\to F^{(0)}_\bullet$ is not null-homotopic, and hence $\psi \colon M'\to M$ is a nonzero morphism.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Chain the one-step lemma along $d=d^0<\dots<d^r=d'$ and compose; surjectivity in position $k$ survives composition, so $\psi\ne 0$.

nodes.name: Interpolate a chain of degree sequences
nodes.statement: Set $r:=\sum_{j=0}^n d_j'-d_j$. We may construct a sequence of degree sequences $d=:d^0<d^1<\dots <d^r:=d'$ such that $d^j$ and $d^{j+1}$ satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} for any $j$. Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} yields a nonzero morphism \[ \phi^{(j+1)} \colon M(d^{j+1})\otimes V\to M(d^j) \] for any $j=1, \dots, r$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Build a chain of degree sequences from $d$ to $d'$ each differing by one, and apply the lemma to each link.

nodes.name: Compose the one-step morphisms
nodes.statement: If we set $M^{(j)}:=M(d^j)\otimes V^{\otimes j}$, and we set $\psi^{(j+1)}$ to be the natural map \[ \psi^{(j+1)} \colon M^{(j+1)}\to M^{(j)} \] given by $\phi^{(j)}\otimes \text{id}_V^{\otimes j}$, then we may compose the map $\psi^{(j+1)}$ with the map $\psi^{(j)}$.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Tensor by $V^{\otimes j}$ so the one-step maps become composable.

nodes.name: Nonvanishing of the composite
nodes.statement: Let $M:=M^{(0)}=M(d),$ and let $M':=M^{(r)}=M(d')\otimes V^{\otimes r}$. We then have an equivariant map $\psi:=\psi^{(1)}\circ \dots \circ \psi^{(r)} \colon M'\to M$, and we must finally show that $\psi$ is nonzero. Let $F^{(j)}_\bullet$ be the minimal free resolution of $M^{(j)}$. Since $d_k=d_k'$, it follows that $d^{(j)}_k=d^{(j+1)}_k$ for all $j$. Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} then implies that we can choose each $\phi^{(j+1)}$ such that the map $\psi^{(j+1)}$ induces a surjection $F^{(j+1)}_k\to F^{(j)}_k$. Since the composition of surjective maps is surjective, it follows that the map $F^{(r)}_k\to F^{(0)}_k$ induced by $\psi$ is surjective. Since $F^{(0)}_\bullet$ is a minimal free resolution, we conclude that the map of complexes $F^{(r)}_\bullet\to F^{(0)}_\bullet$ is not null-homotopic, and hence $\psi \colon M'\to M$ is a nonzero morphism.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Each link is surjective in homological position $k$, so the composite is too, hence not null-homotopic.

nodes.name: A simpler variant using $\Sym^N V$
nodes.statement: By introducing a variant of Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules}, we may simplify the construction used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:eqvtmodules}. Let $d$ and $d'$ be two degree sequences such that $d_i'=d_i+N$, and $d_j'=d_j$ for all $j\ne i$. Iteratively applying Lemma~\ref{lemma:eqvtmodules} yields a morphism $\phi \colon M(d')\otimes V^{\otimes N}\to M(d)$. Since $\ch(\Bbbk)=0$, we have an inclusion $\iota \colon \Sym^N V\to V^{\otimes N}$, and we let $\psi$ be the morphism induced by composing $\phi$ and $\text{id}_{M(d')}\otimes \iota$. Let $F_\bullet'$ and $F_\bullet$ be the minimal free resolutions of $M(d')\otimes \Sym^N V$ and $M(d)$ respectively. The map $F_j'\to F_j$ induced by $\psi$ is induced by the equivariant map of vector spaces \[ \Sc_{\lambda(d')}V\otimes \Sym^NV\to \Sc_{\lambda(d)}V. \] This map is surjective because it is a projection onto one of the factors in the Pieri rule decomposition of $\Sc_{\lambda(d')}V\otimes \Sym^NV$. This simplifies the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:eqvtmodules} as follows. Let $i_1 > \cdots > i_\ell$ be the indices for which $d$ and $d'$ differ. By iteratively applying the construction outlined in this remark, we may construct the desired modules and nonzero morphism in $\ell$ steps. Since $\ell$ can be far smaller than $r:=\sum_{j=0}^n d_j'-d_j$, this variant is useful for computing examples such as Example~\ref{ex:big eqvt}.
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $V^{\otimes N}$ by $\Sym^N V$ lets the construction be done in $\ell$ steps, one per differing index.

nodes.name: Equivariant example with $n=4$, $d=(0,2,3,6,7)$, $d'=(1,2,5,6,10)$
nodes.statement: We illustrate Theorem~\ref{theorem:eqvtmodules} with $n=4$, $d = (0,2,3,6,7)$, and $d' = (1,2,5,6,10)$. Using the notation of Remark~\ref{rmk:simpler}, $d^{(1)} = (0,2,3,6,10)$, $d^{(2)} = (0,2,5,6,10)$. Following the same conventions as in Example~\ref{example:eqvtres1}, the corresponding resolutions are given in Figure~\ref{fig:big diagram}. Notice that $d_3=6=d_3'$. Focusing on the third terms of the resolutions, we see that the maps are simply projections from Pieri's rule. In particular, these maps are surjective and therefore nonzero. \qedhere
nodes.section: 4 Equivariant construction of morphisms between modules with pure resolutions
nodes.statement_short: A four-step Young-diagram illustration of the equivariant theorem, with the maps in position $3$ being Pieri projections.

nodes.name: Cohomology table
nodes.statement: Let $\EE$ be a coherent sheaf on $\PP^{n-1}$. The \defi{cohomology table} of $\EE$ is a table with rows indexed by $\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ and columns indexed by $\ZZ$, such that the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $\dim_\Bbbk \Hs^i(\PP^{n-1}, \EE(j-i))$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
differentia: with rows indexed by $\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ and columns indexed by $\ZZ$
the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $\dim_\Bbbk \Hs^i(\PP^{n-1}, \EE(j-i))$

nodes.name: Root sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence $f=(f_1, \dots, f_{n-1})\in \left(\ZZ\cup\{-\infty\}\right)^{n-1}$ is called a \defi{root sequence} for $\PP^{n-1}$ if $f_i<f_{i-1}$ for all $i$ (with the convention that $-\infty<-\infty$).
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences

nodes.name: Length of a root sequence
nodes.statement: The \defi{length} of $f$, denoted $\ell(f)$, is the largest integer $t$ such that $f_t$ is finite.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences

nodes.name: Supernatural sheaf of type $f$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a root sequence for $\PP^{n-1}$. A sheaf $\EE$ on $\PP^{n-1}$ is \defi{supernatural of type} $f=(f_1, \dots, f_{n-1})$ if the following are satisfied: \begin{asparaenum} \item The dimension of $\Supp \EE$ is $\ell(f)$. \item For all $j\in \mathbb Z$, there exists at most one $i$ such that $\dim_\Bbbk \Hs^i(\PP^{n-1}, \EE(j))\ne 0$. \item The Hilbert polynomial of $\EE$ has roots $f_1, \dots, f_{\ell(f)}$. \end{asparaenum} Dropping the reference to its root sequence, we also say that $\EE$ is a \defi{supernatural sheaf} (or a \defi{supernatural vector bundle} if it is locally free).
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: A sheaf is supernatural of type $f$ when its support has dimension $\ell(f)$, each twist has at most one nonvanishing cohomology group, and its Hilbert polynomial has roots $f_1,\dots,f_{\ell(f)}$.
differentia: For all $j\in \mathbb Z$, there exists at most one $i$ such that $\dim_\Bbbk \Hs^i(\PP^{n-1}, \EE(j))\ne 0$.
The Hilbert polynomial of $\EE$ has roots $f_1, \dots, f_{\ell(f)}$.

nodes.name: Existence of supernatural sheaves
nodes.statement: For every root sequence $f$, there exists a supernatural sheaf of type $f$~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~0.4}.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
conclusions: there exists a supernatural sheaf of type $f$

nodes.name: Positive decomposition of cohomology tables
nodes.statement: Moreover, the cohomology table of any coherent sheaf can be written as a positive real combination of cohomology tables of supernatural sheaves~\cite{EiScSupNat09}*{Theorem~0.1}.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
conclusions: the cohomology table ... can be written as a positive real combination of cohomology tables of supernatural sheaves

nodes.name: Cone of cohomology tables
nodes.statement: The \defi{cone of cohomology tables} for $\PP^{n-1}$ is the convex cone inside $\prod_{j \in \ZZ}\RR^n$ generated by cohomology tables of coherent sheaves on $\PP^{n-1}$. Each root sequence $f$ corresponds to a unique extremal ray of this cone, which we denote by $\rho_f$, and every extremal ray is of the form $\rho_f$ for some root sequence $f$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
differentia: generated by cohomology tables of coherent sheaves on $\PP^{n-1}$

nodes.name: Partial order on root sequences
nodes.statement: For two root sequences $f$ and $f'$, we say that $f\preceq f'$ and that $\rho_f \preceq \rho_{f'}$ if $f_i\leq f_i'$ for all $i$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences

nodes.name: Simplicial fan structure on the cone of cohomology tables
nodes.statement: This partial order induces a simplicial fan structure on the cone of cohomology tables, where simplices correspond to chains of root sequences under the partial order $\preceq$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences

nodes.name: Nonzero homomorphism implies comparability of root sequences
nodes.statement: Let $\EE$ and $\EE'$ be supernatural sheaves of types $f$ and $f'$ respectively. If $\Hom(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$, then $f\preceq f'$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero map $\EE'\to\EE$ between supernatural sheaves forces $f\preceq f'$.
assumptions: Let $\EE$ and $\EE'$ be supernatural sheaves of types $f$ and $f'$ respectively.

nodes.name: Proof of the reverse implication for root sequences
nodes.statement: Let $\tate(\EE)$ and $\tate(\EE')$ denote the Tate resolutions of $\EE$ and $\EE'$~\cite{EiFlScExterior03}*{\S4}. These are doubly infinite acyclic complexes over the exterior algebra $\Lambda$, which is Koszul dual to $S$ and has generators in degree $-1$. Since $\Hom(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$, there is a map $\phi\colon \tate(\EE') \to \tate(\EE)$ that is not null-homotopic. Observe that for every cohomological degree $j$, $\phi^j \colon \tate(\EE')^j \to \tate(\EE)^j$ is nonzero. First, if $\phi^j=0$ for some $j$, then, we may take $\phi^k=0$ for all $k < j$. Secondly, if $k > j$, then after applying $\Hom_{\Lambda}(-, \Lambda)$ (which is exact because $\Lambda$ is self-injective), we can take $\phi^k$ to be zero. By~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~6.4}, we see that all the minimal generators of $T(\EE)^j$ (respectively, $T(\EE')^j$) are of a single degree $i$ (respectively, $i'$). (This is equivalent to stating that every column of the cohomology table of $\EE$ and $\EE'$ contains precisely one nonzero entry.) Since $\phi^j$ is nonzero and $\Lambda$ is generated in elements of degree $-1$, we see that $i' \leq i$. Now, again by~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~6.4}, $f \preceq f'$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: Pass to Tate resolutions over the exterior algebra: the induced map is nonzero in every cohomological degree, and the single-degree generator property forces $f \preceq f'$.

nodes.name: Pass to Tate resolutions
nodes.statement: Let $\tate(\EE)$ and $\tate(\EE')$ denote the Tate resolutions of $\EE$ and $\EE'$~\cite{EiFlScExterior03}*{\S4}. These are doubly infinite acyclic complexes over the exterior algebra $\Lambda$, which is Koszul dual to $S$ and has generators in degree $-1$. Since $\Hom(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$, there is a map $\phi\colon \tate(\EE') \to \tate(\EE)$ that is not null-homotopic.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: Replace the sheaf map by a non-null-homotopic map of Tate resolutions over $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Each $\phi^j$ is nonzero
nodes.statement: Observe that for every cohomological degree $j$, $\phi^j \colon \tate(\EE')^j \to \tate(\EE)^j$ is nonzero. First, if $\phi^j=0$ for some $j$, then, we may take $\phi^k=0$ for all $k < j$. Secondly, if $k > j$, then after applying $\Hom_{\Lambda}(-, \Lambda)$ (which is exact because $\Lambda$ is self-injective), we can take $\phi^k$ to be zero.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: If some $\phi^j$ vanished, self-injectivity of $\Lambda$ would let all components be made zero.

nodes.name: Compare generator degrees to conclude
nodes.statement: By~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~6.4}, we see that all the minimal generators of $T(\EE)^j$ (respectively, $T(\EE')^j$) are of a single degree $i$ (respectively, $i'$). (This is equivalent to stating that every column of the cohomology table of $\EE$ and $\EE'$ contains precisely one nonzero entry.) Since $\phi^j$ is nonzero and $\Lambda$ is generated in elements of degree $-1$, we see that $i' \leq i$. Now, again by~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~6.4}, $f \preceq f'$.
nodes.section: 5 The poset of root sequences
nodes.statement_short: Single-degree generators plus nonvanishing of $\phi^j$ give $i'\le i$, hence $f\preceq f'$.

nodes.name: Existence of a nonzero morphism between supernatural sheaves
nodes.statement: Let $f\preceq f'$ be two root sequences. Then there exist supernatural sheaves $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.

nodes.statement_short: Comparable root sequences are realized by supernatural sheaves admitting a nonzero morphism $\EE'\to\EE$.
assumptions: Let $f\preceq f'$ be two root sequences.
conclusions: there exist supernatural sheaves $\EE$ and $\EE'$ of types $f$ and $f'$, respectively, with $\Hom(\EE',\EE)\ne 0$.

nodes.statement: For the purposes of exposition, we separate the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main:root} into two cases (with $\ell(f) = \ell(f')$ and with $\ell(f) < \ell(f')$), and handle these cases in Propositions~\ref{propn:rootSameLength} and~\ref{propn:rootDiffLength} respectively. Examples~\ref{ex:1} and ~\ref{ex:root:diff:lengths} illustrate the essential ideas behind the proof in each case.

nodes.name: Construction of a nonzero map between supernatural sheaves of equal length
nodes.statement: We now outline our approach to construct a nonzero map between supernatural sheaves on $\PP^s$ of types $f\preceq f'$ in the case that $\ell(f) = \ell(f') = s$. This uses the proof of~\cite{EiScConjOfBS07}*{Theorem~6.1}. \begin{enumerate} \item Construct a finite map $\pi\colon \PP^{1\times s}\to \PP^{s}$. \item Choose appropriate line bundles $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal L'$ on $\PP^{1\times s}$ so that $\pi_* \mathcal L$ and $\pi_*\mathcal L'$ are supernatural vector bundles of the desired types. \item When $\ell(f) = \ell(f') = s$, construct a morphism $\mathcal L' \stackrel{\phi}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal L$ such that $\pi_* \phi$ is nonzero. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Nonzero morphism of supernatural bundles for $n=5$, equal lengths
nodes.statement: Here we find a nonzero morphism $\EE_{f'}\to \EE_{f}$ that is the direct image of a morphism of line bundles on $\PP^{1\times (n-1)}$. Let $n=5$ and $f:=(-2,-3,-4,-5) \preceq f':=(-1,-2,-3,-4)$. The map $\pi\colon \PP^{1\times 4}\to \PP^4$ is finite of degree $4!=24$. Following steps \eqref{enum:snvbConstEqLenFinMap} and \eqref{enum:snvbConstEqLenPushFwd} as outlined above, we set $\EE:=\EE_{f}=\pi_* \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(1,2,3,4)$ and $\EE':=\EE_{f'}=\pi_* \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(0,1,2,3)$. There is a natural inclusion \begin{equation} \pi_* \sheafHom_{\PP^{1\times 4}}\left( \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(0,1,2,3), \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(1,2,3,4)\right)\subseteq \sheafHom_{\PP^4}\left( \EE', \EE \right), \end{equation} which induces an inclusion of global sections (see Remark~\ref{rmk:inclusion}). Therefore \begin{align*} \Hom(\EE', \EE)&\supseteq \Hs^0\left(\PP^4, \pi_* \sheafHom_{\PP^{1\times 4}}\left( \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(0,1,2,3), \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(1,2,3,4)\right) \right)\\ &= \Hs^0(\PP^{1\times 4}, \cO_{\PP^{1\times 4}}(1,1,1,1))\\ &\simeq\Bbbk^{16}. \end{align*} We thus conclude that $\Hom(\EE', \EE)\ne 0$. The inclusion \eqref{equation:inclGlobalSec} is strict. Note that, by definition, neither $\EE'$ nor $\EE$ has intermediate cohomology, and hence, by Horrocks' Splitting Criterion, both $\EE$ and $\EE'$ must split as the sum of line bundles. Thus $\EE'=\cO_{\PP^4}^{24}$ and $\EE=\cO_{\PP^4}(1)^{24}$, and it follows that $\Hom(\EE',\EE)=\Hs^0(\PP^4,\cO(1)^{576}) \simeq \Bbbk^{2880}$.
nodes.section: 6 Construction of morphisms between supernatural sheaves
nodes.statement_short: For $f=(-2,-3,-4,-5)\preceq f'=(-1,-2,-3,-4)$ the pushforward bundles are $\cO^{24}$ and $\cO(1)^{24}$, with a $2880$-dimensional Hom space.

nodes.name: Horrocks' Splitting Criterion
nodes.statement: Note that, by definition, neither $\EE'$ nor $\EE$ has intermediate cohomology, and hence, by Horrocks' Splitting Criterion, both $\EE$ and $\EE'$ must split as the sum of line bundles.
nodes.section: 6 Construction of morphisms between supernatural sheaves
conclusions: both $\EE$ and $\EE'$ must split as the sum of line bundles

nodes.name: Pushforward of sheaf Hom embeds in sheaf Hom of pushforwards
nodes.statement: Let $\pi\colon\PP^{1\times s} \to \PP^s$ be as in \eqref{enum:snvbConstEqLenFinMap}. For coherent sheaves $\FF$ and $\GG$ on $\PP^{1\times s}$, we have \[ \pi_* \sheafHom_{\cO_{\PP^{1\times s}}}(\FF,\GG) \subseteq \sheafHom_{\cO_{\PP^s}}(\pi_*\FF,\pi_*\GG). \] Indeed, this can be checked locally. Let $U \subseteq \PP^s$ be an affine open subset, and write $A = \Hs^0(U, \cO_{\PP^s})$ and $B = \Hs^0(U, \pi_*\cO_{\PP^{1\times s}})$. For all $B$-modules $M$ and $N$, every nonzero $B$-module homomorphism is also a nonzero $A$-module homomorphism via the map $A \rightarrow B$. Injectivity is immediate.
nodes.section: 6 Construction of morphisms between supernatural sheaves
nodes.statement_short: Locally, a nonzero $B$-module map is a nonzero $A$-module map, giving the inclusion $\pi_*\sheafHom(\FF,\GG)\subseteq\sheafHom(\pi_*\FF,\pi_*\GG)$.

nodes.name: Supernaturality is preserved by a linear closed immersion
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\beta \colon \PP^s \to \PP^{n-1}$ is a closed immersion as a linear subvariety. Let $\EE$ be a coherent sheaf on $\PP^s$. It follows from the projection formula and from the finiteness of $\beta$ that $\EE$ is a supernatural sheaf on $\PP^s$ of type $(f_1, \ldots, f_s)$ if and only if $\beta_*\EE$ is a supernatural sheaf on $\PP^{n-1}$ of type $(f_1, \ldots, f_s, -\infty, \ldots, -\infty)$.
nodes.section: 6 Construction of morphisms between supernatural sheaves
nodes.statement_short: Pushing forward along a linear embedding turns a supernatural sheaf of type $(f_1,\dots,f_s)$ into one of type $(f_1,\dots,f_s,-\infty,\dots,-\infty)$.

nodes.name: The equal-length case of the root-sequence theorem
nodes.statement: If $\ell(f) = \ell(f')$, then Theorem~\ref{thm:main:root} holds.

nodes.name: Proof of the equal-length case
nodes.statement:
We first reduce to the case $\ell(f')=n-1$. Let $ eta\colon\PP^{\ell(f')} 	o \PP^{n-1}$ be a closed immersion as a linear subvariety. Let $\ell(f')=s$ and write $f=(f_1, \dots, f_s, -\infty, \dots, -\infty)$ and $f'=(f_1', \dots, f_s', -\infty, \dots, -\infty)$. Assume that $\EE$ and $\EE'$ are supernatural sheaves of type $(f_1, \dots, f_s)$ and $(f'_1, \dots, f_s')$ on $\PP^{s}$ and that $\Hom(\EE', \EE)
e 0$. Then, by Remark~ef{remark:pushFwdSupNat}, $ eta_*\EE$ and $ eta_*\EE'$ are supernatural sheaves of types $f$ and $f'$, and $\Hom( eta_*\EE',  eta_*\EE) 
eq 0$. We may thus assume that $\ell(f')=n-1$. Let $\mathbf{1} := (1,\dots,1) \in\ZZ^{n-1}$. Let $\pi\colon \PP^{1 	imes (n-1)} 	o \PP^{n-1}$ be the morphism given by the forms $g_p$ defined in~\eqref{eqn:fp} (with $s=n-1$). Let $\EE := \EE_f= \pi_* \cO(-f-\mathbf 1)$ and $\EE' := \EE_{f'}= \pi_*\cO(-f'-\mathbf{1})$. Remark~ef{rmk:inclusion} shows that \[ \Hs^0\left(\PP^{n-1}, \pi_* \sheafHom_{\PP^{1	imes (n-1)}}\left( \cO(-f'-\mathbf{1}), \cO(-f-\mathbf{1}) ight) ight) \subseteq \Hom_{\PP^{n-1}}(\EE',\EE). \] Note that $\sheafHom_{\PP^{1	imes (n-1)}}\left( \cO(-f'-\mathbf{1}), \cO(-f-\mathbf{1}) ight) = \cO( f' - f )$. Since $f \preceq f'$, we have that $\Hs^0(\PP^{1	imes (n-1)}, \cO( f'- f ))
e 0$, and thus $\Hom_{\PP^{n-1}}(\EE',\EE)
